talks.title: Keynote
talks.teaser: Revisits four application security beliefs that turned out wrong, and why incentives and trade-offs matter more.
talks.summary:
The keynote opens with a note that the views are personal rather than those of the speaker's employer, then frames the talk as a look at application security beliefs that proved mistaken. The speaker argues that success stories tend to skip what went wrong, and that unexamined assumptions about how controls behave are often the real source of risk.

The middle covers four beliefs the speaker has dropped. First, that organizations will take up application security purely out of principle: security competes for limited engineering time and budget, and change tends to come from breaches, compliance rules, software bill of materials requirements and customer contract demands. Second, that every developer should become a security expert through broad principles training; targeted, code-level guidance in the languages teams actually use is more practical. Third, that only developers belong in the field, when auditors, product managers and writers are needed too. Fourth, that certifications have little value, overlooking how useful they are for people without degrees.

The closing thread is that the speaker had assumed others shared their background and priorities. The takeaway is to seek out people who disagree, take negative feedback seriously, and recognize that this work is a long effort best done together.

talks.title: Invited Speaker
talks.teaser: Explains how cyber insurance coverage, exclusions and privilege rules shape what a breach costs an organization.
talks.summary:
This session walks security and compliance staff through cyber insurance, with the speaker noting that it is educational rather than legal advice. It opens with risk management: accepting, avoiding, mitigating or transferring risk, with insurance sitting in the mitigation and transfer categories. The speaker separates first-party losses, which hit the organization itself, from third-party liability for harm caused to others, and notes that internal remediation and internal investigation costs usually stay with the company.

The middle covers typical coverage lines such as regulatory defense and fines, notification, public relations, credit monitoring, outside incident response, ransomware payments and lost income. Exclusions get the most attention, including new-or-should-have-known clauses, breach-of-contract exclusions, war limits and sublimits that may or may not stack. Incident handling is central: a small control group, outside counsel hiring a separate forensics firm under a specific scope, and tight distribution of the report help protect work product. Two cases contrast a protected report with one that lost protection. Ransomware brings sanctions screening for payments, insurer disputes over voluntary payments and rising deductibles.

The takeaways are to review exclusions against actual controls, pre-approve response vendors with the insurer, settle in advance who holds the policy and who to call, and test restores, since recovery can take weeks. Small organizations should carry at least some coverage.

talks.title: Using the Threat Modeling Manifesto to Build an Enterprise Threat Modeling Program
talks.teaser: Shows how the Threat Modeling Manifesto can anchor a threat modeling program that scales beyond a small specialist group.
talks.summary:
The session starts from a common problem: most organizations agree threat modeling matters, but scaling it from a handful of experts to many engineering teams is hard. Centralized security teams and appointed champions tend to end up with a growing backlog of reviews they cannot finish. The speaker introduces the Threat Modeling Manifesto, written by a group of about fifteen practitioners, and explains its working definition of threat modeling as analyzing representations of a system to surface security and privacy concerns. The document borrows its structure from the Agile manifesto, listing values such as finding and fixing design issues over checkbox compliance, and people collaborating over process and tools.

The middle of the talk covers the principles, along with anti-patterns to avoid, such as the hero threat modeler and perfect representation, and positive patterns such as a systematic approach, creative brainstorming with varied viewpoints, and choosing tools only after the process is understood. The speaker then offers a set of tips for an enterprise program. These include a repeatable process built around scope and the four key questions, embedding the work in the secure development lifecycle and existing tools, building threat modeling champions and internal coaches, teaching through hands-on workshops, and drawing on STRIDE, ASVS, CWE and ATT&CK as sources of threats. Mitigations are presented as the real measure of value.

The closing takeaway is to model individual features first, keep quality checks supportive rather than punitive, and report results in terms stakeholders understand. The audience questions touched on feature-level versus whole-system models and on how to present threats and risk to executives.

talks.title: Climbing AppSec Mountains (and how to summit)
talks.teaser: Explains how enterprise appsec teams get blocked by their own companies and what helps them succeed.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a fictional application security engineer, Ned, who is asked to build an internal appsec team at a large enterprise. His mandate covers securing existing and future code, shifting security earlier in development, and training developers. The speaker, who has worked on both development and appsec sides at large companies, uses Ned's situation to walk through the obstacles that pile up: aging scanners and firewalls, alert fatigue, acquisitions that bring in weak software, application portfolios running into the hundreds or thousands, and fast-changing languages and frameworks.

The middle section turns to fixes. The speaker suggests pairing interactive testing and runtime protection with a narrower, blocking-mode web firewall, so feedback arrives faster and with fewer false alarms. Appsec can also join acquisition reviews by putting the cost of inherited flaws into numbers. For new technology, an acceptable use policy reviewed by an architecture board lets teams innovate while still meeting standards. Workplace churn is handled with burn lists, sweeps for default and test credentials, and remote secure coding training that developers complete before touching code, backed by prebuilt secure templates.

The closing part addresses inflexible developers. The speaker argues that appsec should sit outside engineering, build real working relationships through shared meals, games, capture-the-flag contests and hackathons, and treat developers as partners rather than opponents. The Q&A touches on false positives from development-only dependencies and on supply chain exposure, with the advice that appsec staff understand enough code to challenge findings credibly.

talks.title: Insiders Guide to Mobile AppSec with OWASP MASVS
talks.teaser: Walks through the OWASP MASVS to show where mobile apps most often fail and how to test them.
talks.summary:
The talk is a guided tour of the OWASP Mobile Application Security Verification Standard, aimed at web security practitioners who are moving into mobile testing. It starts from the premise that a mobile app runs on a hostile, user-controlled device, so reversing and tampering should be assumed. Benchmark data from scanned app store releases is used to show that most apps carry security issues, with insecure data storage and network communication among the most frequent findings, and insecure coding and authentication also appearing often.

The middle of the session groups MASVS guidance by the sensitivity of the data an app handles. It covers keeping data off the device, avoiding sensitive values in query strings and logs, checking that certificate pinning and platform network settings are actually applied, and treating anti-tampering as added friction rather than a fix. The speaker argues for moving sensitive logic and key generation to the server, and for building apps with testability in mind so that automated tools can cover much of the security test suite. Tooling such as Frida, Radare, proxies and rooted or jailbroken test devices is mentioned as part of a practical toolkit.

The closing section covers software bill of materials work through CycloneDX, and an IoT-focused certification built from MASVS for mobile apps that talk to connected devices. The main takeaways are to threat model early, test on real devices, scrutinise third-party libraries, and use the free MASVS and MSTG resources as a starting point.

talks.title: How security can keep pace with continuously evolving cloud-native applications
talks.teaser: Shows how security teams can keep pace with cloud-native architectures that change release by release through infrastructure as code.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at a trend where cloud application architectures change release over release, sometimes sprint over sprint, because infrastructure is now written as code in tools such as Terraform and CloudFormation. Ownership of that code is shifting to development teams, and the speaker notes that security reviews often fall out of date before a design ships. Cloud providers also release features quickly, sometimes before their security controls are complete.

The middle of the talk covers responses. Security teams are advised to make guidance accessible to developers through training, to build reusable design patterns as Terraform templates, and to take part in design and threat modeling early. Automation is presented as the way to scale small teams: scanning infrastructure code in the pipeline, reporting the reason for each finding and the specific setting to change, and detecting drift between code and deployed resources. Restricting console and CLI changes so the pipeline is the only path is described as the most effective control, with break-glass access needed during incidents.

A live demo runs a scanning integration in GitHub Actions against a small Terraform project containing an API gateway, a Lambda function, S3 buckets and a KMS key. After a Kinesis stream and SQS queue are added from a public example, the scan flags key management gaps and explains how to fix them. The speaker closes by showing how changing a data-sensitivity attribute can raise requirements as a prototype matures, and urges combining training, patterns, automation and feedback loops.

talks.title: Introduction to inner-loop security. Shifting left, but better.
talks.teaser: Argues that security testing belongs in the developer's inner loop and offers a model for secure-by-design development.
talks.summary:
The talk traces "shift left" back to a 2001 article about bringing QA into development, then argues that the idea has drifted into tooling pushed onto developers with little regard for their workload. Examples include IDE plugins nobody uses, training that does not stick, and performance reviews that ignore security.

To offer an alternative, the talk adapts the inner and outer loop model from software delivery. The inner loop covers coding, building, testing and committing on a developer's machine, while the outer loop starts at the pull request and holds pipelines, scanners and vulnerability management. Each common AppSec activity is judged by the friction it adds to developer flow. Static analysis, DAST, manual pen testing and software composition analysis mostly land in the outer loop because they are slow, need a running application, or generate noise. Lightweight dependency checks, fast control tests and pre-commit hooks are presented as better inner-loop candidates.

The conclusion is that no universal balance of friction exists, so teams should weigh each control's cost to developers. Reporting should focus on validating security controls rather than chasing long vulnerability lists, with the aim of making the secure option the easy one.

talks.title: What security engineers can learn from DevSecOps
talks.teaser: Explains how security engineers can partner with developers to build customer-facing features and learn software practices.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that DevSecOps should run in both directions: developers learn security, and security engineers should learn how software gets built and shipped. The speaker suggests starting with small, low-priority bugs from the vulnerability backlog. Doing that shows how much work a seemingly simple fix takes, including testing, code review and deployment, and it builds empathy with engineers and personal connections across teams.

The middle covers moving from bug fixes to customer-facing security features, using examples such as a password strength meter, multi-factor authentication and SCIM user provisioning. Security features can serve customers better and open revenue in business-to-business sales. The speaker recommends finding a team already working on something, agreeing on a shared goal and long-term ownership, and justifying funding with questionnaire data, customer contract values and product metrics. Design docs should follow the company template and include reviewers, referenced standards, a glossary, prioritised requirements, diagrams, risks and an early security review.

The closing advice covers pull requests kept short and explained for future readers, thorough tests and manual test notes, planned rollback steps, staggered feature-flag rollouts, and dashboards wired to alerts. Security staff should also share what they learned with the teams they worked with and credit collaborators. The main takeaway is that learning how a company writes and maintains software makes a security engineer better at the job, even without a long-term software career.

talks.title: The Final Frontier, Automating DYNAMIC Security Testing
talks.teaser: Explains how to automate dynamic application security testing in pipelines, weighing trade-offs and running a live Docker demo.
talks.summary:
The talk takes on dynamic application security testing (DAST), which the speakers describe as the hardest part of security automation to get right. They start by contrasting static and dynamic testing, then lay out the obstacles that tend to appear: staging environments that drift from production, different inline controls such as WAFs, mismatched data, and the difficulty of provisioning test accounts for authenticated scans.

The middle section covers the decisions that shape a scan. Unauthenticated scans are simpler and easier to get approved, while authenticated scans reach much more of the application but need careful credential and login handling. Full crawls are thorough but slow, and targeted crawls focus on the riskiest areas. The speakers frame adoption as a maturity path, moving from a proof of concept to tuning a scanner and then to scheduled, hands-off runs. They also discuss static versus ephemeral environments, configuration management, containers, and tailoring reports for developers versus auditors.

The closing part is a live demo in which a Docker Compose setup launches an SSL checker and OWASP ZAP against a deliberately vulnerable web application. Results are written to a shared volume and imported into DefectDojo. Practical takeaways include starting with a narrow scope, using open-source tools to prove value before buying, checking whether a commercial scanner's API really supports automation, and keeping scan duration in line with commit frequency. Findings should also flow into the tools developers already use rather than arriving as large PDFs.

talks.title: SSL Hell
talks.teaser: Shows how ACME and cert-manager automate issuing and renewing TLS certificates for many Kubernetes microservices.
talks.summary:
The talk starts with the cost of managing TLS certificates by hand across many microservices. The speakers, who work on an identity management product on AWS and GCP, describe staging outages caused by misconfigured or expired certificates. They recall an April outage at Epic Games, where one expired wildcard certificate deployed across hundreds of backend servers caused a multi-hour disruption, and they note that manual tracking often still relies on spreadsheets.

The middle section introduces ACME as a protocol for automated issuance and renewal. A client requests a certificate and proves control of a domain through an HTTP or DNS challenge before the certificate authority signs it. A live demo runs a command-line ACME client against an nginx server using Let's Encrypt, followed by manual HTTP and DNS challenge flows.

The final part covers cert-manager, a Kubernetes add-on that applies this process across services. Issuers, either namespace-scoped or cluster-wide, define the ACME provider and DNS solver, while certificate resources list domains and a renewal window, such as 15 days before expiry. Results land in Kubernetes secrets, optionally as Java keystores or PKCS#12 files, and ingress controllers pick them up. The speakers flag limitations: it only runs on Kubernetes, private keys sit in secrets that need protection, the controller itself must be monitored after a renewal bug they hit, and Let's Encrypt enforces per-domain issuance limits that separate environments under one domain can exhaust quickly.

talks.title: The Software Security Testing Lifecycle: The framework testers need
talks.teaser: Presents a phased framework that places security testing alongside each stage of the software development lifecycle.
talks.summary:
The speaker argues that security testing is usually bolted on late, so findings arrive as a list of alerts that developers push back on. To address this, the talk introduces the Software Security Testing Lifecycle, a framework meant to supplement an existing secure development lifecycle rather than replace it. It is aimed at testers and at anyone else who influences how a product is built.

The walk-through moves phase by phase. It starts with security requirements drawn from laws, business expectations and internal policy. Threat modeling follows, with testers in the room, and STRIDE pairs each threat with the control meant to stop it. The testing strategy then maps every threat and control to a unit test, an automated scan or a manual check. Security unit tests take an attacker's view instead of only confirming the happy path. Scanners need customizing for the application or they generate noise, and fuzz targets keep fuzzing limited to interfaces named in the threat model.

The final stage is hands-on validation of scanner findings and of the controls identified in threat modeling. Testers define pass and fail criteria in advance, confirm each issue, and find the root cause, so the fix is a code change, a corrected control or a new control. Retesting checks that the fix did not introduce a new weakness. The main takeaway is that the first three steps, covering requirements, threat modeling and strategy, give a team a usable plan even with limited resources, and the rest can be scaled to the project.

talks.title: Security Observability 101: Thinking Inside the Box!
talks.teaser: Shows how runtime instrumentation in Java can expose sensors for SQL, crypto, access control and expression injection.
talks.summary:
Jeff Williams opens by arguing that software is hard to secure because it runs as a black box, and that most application security work relies on after-the-fact tools like logs, scans and pen tests that see little of what happens at runtime. He frames instrumentation as a way to watch an application from inside while it runs, pointing to fitness trackers and factory sensors as familiar examples.

The middle of the talk is a live demonstration with JOT, a free and open source Java observability toolkit that attaches as a Java agent and uses YAML rules to place sensors on chosen methods without writing code. He runs a deliberately vulnerable app and captures unprepared SQL statements, logs which encryption algorithms are used across the whole stack, and builds coverage and access control matrices by recording routes, users and role checks as he clicks through pages. He then blocks an expression language injection by prohibiting process execution inside the evaluation scope, and shows that a failing sensor can fail a developer's ordinary test run.

To close, he contrasts this runtime approach with network firewalls and point-in-time scanning, and describes interactive testing and runtime self-protection as commercial versions of the same idea. He also notes that much library code in a typical application never executes, which makes many scanner findings false alarms, and warns that compromised developer machines can inject malicious code into release pipelines. The takeaway is that runtime visibility gives security, development and operations a shared, accurate view of how software behaves.

talks.title: A Hacker's Guide to Blockchain, Smart Contracts, and NFTs
talks.teaser: Explains blockchain, smart contracts, and NFTs from a security angle, covering wallet risks, auditing and emerging threats.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the speaker's take on Facebook renaming itself Meta and pushing into the metaverse, arguing that security teams will soon need to understand blockchain whether they like it or not. It then describes distributed ledgers as replicated, tamper-evident databases and runs the CIA triad against them. Confidentiality is presented as weak on public chains, where balances and transactions can be inspected, while integrity and non-repudiation are seen as strong points. Availability is tied to gas fees, which can make transactions expensive or impractical when a network is congested.

The middle section covers smart contracts as code stored on-chain, usually written in Solidity and called through web3 libraries that work much like a payment API integration. The speaker points to the application binary interface as an attack surface that automated bots scan for misconfigurations, and gives the example of a ticket sale contract with no purchase limit. NFTs are described as ownership records that can pay creators royalties on resale, with speculation about future uses for credentials and logs.

The closing part focuses on threats and defenses. Quantum computing is raised as a possible future risk to private keys, while phishing and social engineering are described as common against wallet holders. A seed phrase is shown to grant full control of a browser-based hot wallet, and the speaker contrasts it with hardware cold wallets. Organizations accepting crypto are urged to plan custody, access control and staff departures before they start taking payments.

talks.title: Doing This One Crazy Thing Will Change Your AppSec Program Forever
talks.teaser: Argues that appsec should prove software is secure with evidence, and proposes security labels to restore buyer trust.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from the gap between what people assume about software and what it actually contains. The speaker points to repeated high-profile breaches and to the same vulnerability classes persisting in the OWASP Top 10 for about two decades as signs that current application security practice is not answering the basic question of whether a product is secure. Drawing on the economics of information asymmetry, he frames software buying as a market where purchasers cannot see how a product was built or tested.

The proposed alternative is to treat security as a running argument. A team identifies its biggest threat first, chooses a primary and a backup defense, and gathers evidence that the defense works, ideally from automated checks in the delivery pipeline. Testing should cover the fully assembled application, because source-only scans miss runtime libraries and configuration and generate false positives. Rather than counting findings, the speaker suggests tracking how quickly vulnerabilities are fixed and how often new ones are introduced. He also demonstrated runtime protection against expression language injection, the flaw behind the Equifax breach, using an open-source tool.

The closing argument is for security labels, comparable to nutrition facts or crash ratings, that summarize the evidence behind a product so buyers can make informed choices. Software bills of materials are one piece of that picture. Audience questions covered whether ASVS levels could serve as a starting point and how threat modeling and certification fit in. The practical takeaway is to tie each control to a specific threat and check it with evidence, rather than running activities out of habit.

talks.title: Developing and Managing an OWASP Project (Projects 101)
talks.teaser: Walks through starting, funding, and retiring an OWASP open source project, from naming and licensing to project levels.
talks.summary:
This high-level introduction is aimed at anyone thinking about launching an OWASP project. It starts with why people create projects, usually out of a love of open source, a wish to share application security knowledge, or a gap that needs tools or documentation, and notes that no security background is required. Before submitting a request, a prospective leader should gather a project name, a classification, an open source license, contact details for co-leaders, a short description and a roadmap. Descriptive names work better than acronyms or "Top 10" style labels.

The talk then covers project types, which are documentation, code and tools, and the builder, breaker and defender categories that a project can combine. Documentation projects usually use a Creative Commons license, while code and tools projects choose an approved open source license. Project pages are built on Jekyll and GitHub Pages from generated templates, and leaders must replace the placeholder text and keep the leader file in its required format. On funding, sponsorship money goes through the foundation, and leaders should get pre-approval before spending. A newer grant program lets projects request funds for specific deliverables. The speaker stressed vendor neutrality: leaders should come from more than one company, sponsors belong on a separate tab, and a project should not be used to upsell a commercial product.

Projects advance from incubator to lab to flagship, with a mature level under discussion, and a committee review decides promotions. Approved projects can use services such as code hosting, meetup tools, graphics and community translation help. A project ends either by passing leadership to another person, which is preferred, or by being archived. The talk closes with resources including the project committee, leader contacts and the community chat, and suggests that student chapters contribute to incubator projects that need help.

talks.title: TMI, the kinds of data your applications are leaking
talks.teaser: Shows how exposed API endpoints, verbose errors and weak authorization leak data and enable account takeover.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with how attackers locate exposed API endpoints. Enumeration starts with DNS lookups for api subdomains, then moves to content discovery tools that rely on large wordlists of common routes. Hunters also check for default paths such as WordPress admin and XML-RPC files, inspect mobile traffic through an intercepting proxy, unpack Android app packages for embedded endpoints, and search public API catalogs and code repositories for specs and leaked keys.

The middle covers recurring mistakes: authentication headers that are not properly enforced, tokens accepted across tenants on a shared platform, registration errors that reveal whether an account exists, and verbose messages that help attackers. Credential stuffing often leads to account takeover, and stored payment data turns that into fraud, alongside gift card balance guessing and inventory hoarding. A live Burp demo showed a modified query parameter returning user records from another community on the same platform, and exposed OpenAPI specs and WordPress manifests gave an attacker a roadmap.

The closing section covers signals of automated abuse, such as one IP address trying thousands of usernames, unusual browser user agents hitting app endpoints, traffic from countries the business never serves, and sequential order number scans. Recommended practices include keeping API specs out of public reach, returning generic error messages, inventorying forgotten endpoints, reviewing logs, and testing apps through a proxy, with a deliberately vulnerable API as a training aid.

talks.title: BRICK'D - Making End User AppSec Training Awesome with building bricks
talks.teaser: Uses brick-building photos and minifigure scenes to make application security training memorable for end users.
talks.summary:
The talk presents a way to make application security training stick with non-technical end users by pairing it with humorous photos of minifigures and custom brick builds. The speaker has used these images with OWASP chapters and Java user groups, and explains that the aim is to bridge gaps between development, security and business teams by giving them a memorable framing instead of dry material.

Much of the talk walks through the OWASP Top 10 categories, each illustrated with a scene. Examples include a builder, breaker and defender to frame team roles, a hiker with a map for security guides, mad scientists and aliens with needles for injection, a superhero with a lasso for supply chain trust, and a spaceman whose helmet keeps breaking for known vulnerable components. Other topics cover insecure design and developer incentives, default configurations and stack-trace exposure, continuous review of aging dependencies, malicious open-source packages, financial impact framing for executives, logging of both good and bad events, and input sanitizing with parameterized queries. It also addresses multi-factor authentication beyond SMS, social engineering such as business email compromise, scam calls targeting older relatives, insider risk, and badge tailgating.

The closing takeaway is that security messaging works better when it is cooperative and tailored to each audience. The speaker invites attendees to discuss adapting the approach with their own teams and chapters.

talks.title: API Security: Is it the new application attack surface and how to secure at enterprise scale?
talks.teaser: Explains how API-driven application architectures widen attack surfaces and outlines controls for securing APIs at enterprise scale.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with how modern web apps are built. Single-page apps make many API calls to back-end services, which return raw JSON that the browser assembles. The speaker argues this moves data handling toward the server and widens the attack surface through more endpoints, microservices reused across use cases, weak object-level authorization, and filtering spread across many layers. Classic issues such as CSRF matter less for stateless calls, while rate limiting becomes more important.

Two real incidents anchor the discussion. A social network's contact-lookup API let callers enumerate phone numbers without rate limits and returned far more personal data than the feature needed. A search company left a staging server connected to production data reachable from the internet, with no inventory of its APIs. Both map to OWASP API Top 10 themes such as broken authorization, excessive data exposure and improper asset management. The protection model classifies APIs by audience and data sensitivity, then applies baseline controls: strong authentication, object-level authorization, key rotation, rate limits, payload encryption, secrets management, bot detection, content inspection, logging and file upload protection.

The closing advice is to design security in from the start. Teams should document abuse cases, return only the data each consumer needs, know who consumes each API, and tailor testing and gateway or WAF policies to sensitive endpoints. Anomaly monitoring complements fixed rate limits, since static thresholds are hard to set well.

talks.title: Manual JavaScript Analysis is a Bug
talks.teaser: Explains how to automate repetitive JavaScript application testing with static and dynamic tools and a staged methodology.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that repetitive manual work in application security is a problem to be engineered away. Drawing on a write-up about two equally skilled engineers, one of whom pulled ahead through iterative automation, the speaker proposes a path: document the steps by hand, convert them into static analysis rules, then build a tool that runs on its own. Freed from routine searching, testers can spend more time on business logic flaws and attack chains.

The middle of the talk covers tooling for modern JavaScript applications. Semgrep rules can locate risky sources and sinks in code, while the DOM Invader feature in Burp tracks canary values from input to dangerous functions in the browser. Blind cross-site scripting is caught with out-of-band callbacks, and endpoints and internal domains are pulled from bundled scripts. Source maps can be restored to original code through developer tools. Regular expressions prone to denial of service are found by pairing Semgrep with the recheck tool, secrets are scanned with Semgrep rules, and dependencies are checked with npm audit, yarn audit and retire.js. A proof-of-concept tool combining these open-source checks was demonstrated on a sample project.

The closing section notes that automation misses things, and that a suspected issue is sometimes better written up as a potential finding than chased for days. The speaker recommends automating any task repeated often and keeping per-library checklists, such as cookie flags for express-session, to guide manual review. The takeaway is to automate both static and dynamic analysis across the browser, proxies and source code.

talks.title: Security while scaling Agile - lessons learned
talks.teaser: Explains how a security team kept its controls working as a product organization moved from waterfall to scaled Agile with SAFe.
talks.summary:
Karen, a principal security architect, describes what happened when a product group moved from waterfall to Agile and then to the Scaled Agile Framework (SAFe). Her security plan of roughly fifty activities per lifecycle stage no longer fit short sprints run by many small teams, and security activities had stopped being scheduled. The talk covers how the security team adapted, the obstacles it met, and what remains unfinished.

The first fix was to regroup the activities into about a dozen backlog stories and build a guided tool that asks teams a series of questions, so each team generates only the security work its change needs. Security requirements were reframed as enablers so product owners could prioritize them, and risk assessment moved to the earliest stages, such as research spikes and program increment planning. Pipeline scanning was pushed toward trunk-based development, though templates for the varied languages and CI systems were still in progress, and threat modeling and risk decisions stayed manual.

The main takeaways are to work directly with engineers, managers and product owners, automate wherever possible, and rely on a champion network, since full-time security staff amounted to about one percent of the engineering population. An audience member from a much larger organization described a similar menu of non-functional requirements, which reinforced the approach.

talks.title: Detection Engineering Methodologies
talks.teaser: Outlines a practical methodology for building, testing and reviewing detection rules, from naming to incident response.
talks.summary:
The talk comes from the lead of a detection program at Atlassian, which started after a red team exercise led leadership to ask for rules that would stop a similar intrusion from happening again. The speaker describes the team's early, loosely organized approach, where detections were tracked in a cluttered table that discouraged analysts from contributing. The group cut its process back to the fields responders actually need, then drew on Palantir's alerting and detection strategy framework to build its own standard.

The middle of the talk walks through that methodology. Each detection records its logic, scope, a MITRE ATT&CK tactic, a short human-readable name, its data source, its strategy, known blind spots and accepted false positives, plus a response runbook. Peer review asks whether an analyst who did not write the rule has enough context to act on its alerts. Automation carries much of the weight: every Splunk search is syntax-checked in a CI/CD pipeline and run daily to catch fields that have changed. Work is planned in four-week cycles focused on one tactic, with mid-cycle check-ins where engineers review each other's detections. Breach readiness documents gather architecture, log sources and contacts for products the team does not know well.

The closing advice is to start small, keep names descriptive, document blind spots rather than hiding them, and adapt any framework to your own environment instead of adopting it unchanged. The Q&A covers build versus buy decisions and the difficulty of enforcing logging standards across development teams.

talks.title: Comparing WAF and RASP, Why?
talks.teaser: Compares web application firewalls with runtime application self-protection and explains where each one fits in defense.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with how much of a modern application is custom code versus third-party components, and why application security struggles to keep pace with the volume of software being written. It then covers web application firewalls, a layer seven control that inspects traffic and blocks suspicious patterns without knowing the application's context. The speaker explains how regex-driven rules produce false positives, need constant tuning, and can be bypassed through encoding and SQL comment tricks, using the recent Confluence OGNL injection as an example.

The talk then turns to runtime application self-protection, which runs inside the application through instrumentation. By tracking untrusted input from its source to sensitive sinks, it can tell whether a query's structure has changed and block only when intent is altered, which keeps alert volume low. The speaker also covers the trade-offs: performance overhead, dependence on specific languages and frameworks, installation by a different team, and application restarts when fixes ship. Payload-list testing is criticized as a poor basis for comparing the two.

The closing argument is that the two technologies complement each other rather than compete, much like seat belts and airbags. A WAF handles things such as DDoS protection and broad perimeter patching, while RASP provides context-aware blocking inside the app. Attendees are encouraged to use both where possible, and the Equifax breach is cited as an example of the gap a faster, layered response could have closed.

talks.title: Cloud security and Compliance
talks.teaser: Surveys cloud security risks and maps AWS shared responsibility and compliance controls for organizations.
talks.summary:
The session opens with the concerns organizations raise about moving to the cloud. The speaker cites a 2021 industry survey of security professionals, in which data leakage, privacy and accidental credential exposure ranked as the top worries, and misconfiguration was described as a persistent problem. Cloud risk is framed as largely similar to on-premises risk, with shadow IT, privileged access and governance gaps singled out as areas that need attention.

The middle of the talk looks at reference models from the Cloud Security Alliance and the difference between IaaS, PaaS and SaaS, since that split determines who controls what. The AWS shared responsibility model is the central example: the customer stays accountable for its data, identities, operating systems and configuration, while the provider covers the underlying infrastructure. The speaker explains SOC 1 and SOC 2 reports, the trust service criteria, and how ISO 27001 and related cloud standards map to controls. A tour of AWS security services, including identity management, logging, monitoring and configuration auditing, is organized around identify, protect and detect.

The closing discussion covers developers who hard-coded long-lived access keys and resisted rotating them. The suggested approach is to tie the change to a compliance requirement, invest in training, and assign a clear business owner to each application so accountability is not left unassigned.

talks.title: Infosec metrics that your bosses will love
talks.teaser: Shows how Twilio's security team turned Jira data into automated, near real-time dashboards for different audiences.
talks.summary:
The speakers begin with why security needs quantified metrics. Without numbers, security is often seen as a cost center, while trends over time can justify headcount and budget. They list measures a security organization can report, including vulnerability age and remediation rates, patch currency, cloud exposure, endpoint agent coverage, incident timelines and phishing results. Their starting point was a manual monthly process: someone gathered data from several tools and Jira, aggregated it in a spreadsheet and answered follow-up questions. The result was stale, hard to scale and not tailored to different audiences.

The middle of the talk covers requirements gathered from executives, engineering managers and product managers, who each needed different detail and did not want another tool to log into. The team added standard Jira fields for vulnerability source, category and business unit, since label-based queries were inconsistent. A Python job collected and normalized ticket data, calculated SLA status and wrote it to a Google Sheet that fed Google Data Studio. Three dashboards followed: a leadership overview, a view for the security team by source and category, and a detailed team view. These were embedded in the internal wiki, with edit rights limited to the security team.

The speakers say executives found the dashboards useful for identifying which business units needed attention, and some engineering teams built their own views from the data. They note limitations, such as a sync problem that sometimes required a manual refresh. Next steps include bringing in data from other security teams and building a risk scorecard per product. The talk closes with sample templates and dummy data shared publicly.

talks.title: JWTs - Patterns & Anti-patterns
talks.teaser: Explores JWT use cases, common anti-patterns and safer alternatives for session and service-to-service authentication.
talks.summary:
The talk gives a practical tour of JSON Web Tokens, starting with their three parts: a header, a claims payload and a signature. It separates terms that people often mix up, such as HTTP cookies, traditional random session keys and stateless tokens, and explains why teams adopt JWTs, mainly to avoid database lookups on every request and to pass identity between internal services.

The middle section walks through common anti-patterns. These include accepting the "none" algorithm, placing sensitive data in claims that anyone can decode, keeping tokens in local storage, using weak or reused HMAC secrets, and issuing tokens with no expiration or no way to revoke them. Revocation tables bring back the database lookups the design was meant to avoid, while homegrown refresh-and-access token schemes and fragile key rotation add complexity with little security gain.

The closing section offers safer approaches. Hardcoding the expected algorithm, relying on maintained libraries, and setting registered claims such as expiration, issuer, subject and key ID all reduce risk. A short-lived deny list in a cache with TTLs can limit the cost of revocation. The speaker suggests that plain session tokens or alternatives such as Macaroons often fit better than JWTs for sessions, and points to RFC 8725 as a best-practice reference.

talks.title: Get funding for your Security Initiatives by thinking like a MBA not a CISSP
talks.teaser: Shows how to frame security spending requests in business terms so that management can judge and fund them.
talks.summary:
Security teams often struggle to win budget because they describe risk in technical terms while executives weigh cost, benefit and business impact. The session opens with the different perspectives of security, IT and business leaders, and why each group tends to focus on different concerns. It then argues that a culture built on fear and blame discourages employees from reporting problems, and that optimism bias makes abstract warnings easy to dismiss.

The middle of the talk covers practical steps. The presenters recommend knowing the audience, especially how finance leaders and the board think, and expressing risk in dollar terms wherever possible. Business impact analysis and tabletop exercises let stakeholders experience a simulated outage or breach, which makes their estimates more realistic. Risk scales should be applied consistently across the organization, and dashboards and key risk indicators only help when they answer questions decision-makers actually ask. Framing work through SWOT analysis or a recognized framework, plus a roadmap and governance to handle change, keeps requests credible over time.

The closing advice is to build a collaborative culture, invite objective outside review, admit known weaknesses openly, and draw on finance colleagues' experience with audits and controls. Attendees leave with a method for turning security initiatives into justified, trackable investments.

talks.title: Your frontier defense
talks.teaser: Compares cloud and self-managed web application firewall options, including ModSecurity, and their operational trade-offs.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the case for a web application firewall as a layer beyond network firewalls, which do not inspect HTTP traffic. The presenters explain how a WAF sits as a reverse proxy in front of backend services, keeps them off the public internet, centralizes TLS settings, and lets teams block, allow or log requests. They recommend running in detection mode before enforcement so rules can be tuned and false positives reduced.

The middle of the talk walks through managed options from AWS, Azure and Google Cloud Armor, showing how web ACLs, rule priority and managed rule groups are configured. It then covers self-managed ModSecurity with Apache and nginx using the OWASP Core Rule Set. The comparison looks at request body inspection limits, response inspection, granular exception handling and control over rule versions, and describes the operational burden of self-managed deployments, including patching, central management and monitoring.

The closing section discusses false positives, reproducing customer-reported blocks and testing coverage as ongoing challenges, and explains why one organization kept an in-house ModSecurity-based setup. The takeaway is to choose a WAF by weighing rule control, operational effort and the team's expertise.

talks.title: Cloud Security Scaled: The Chaos Continues
talks.teaser: Shares lessons from securing cloud migrations at financial firms, covering infrastructure as code checks and basic controls.
talks.summary:
The speakers continue a series on cloud security in regulated finance, drawing on roughly 30 to 40 organizations they have worked with. They present three composite case studies: a large enterprise with hundreds of AWS accounts and thousands of applications, a mid-sized lending firm, and a small blockchain project run by one to three people.

For the large enterprise, the team describes how infrastructure as code let them enforce security policy before deployment. Policy checks written as code, using tools such as Terraform with Sentinel, CloudFormation linting and Semgrep, ran in seconds and caught problems before they reached production. They warn that rules must match how teams actually deploy, and that pre-deployment checks miss resources and relationships that exist only at runtime. For the mid-sized lender, the speakers describe an overhaul of secrets management with HashiCorp Vault, which made rotation easier for developers than the old manual process. The firm then used an OWASP SAMM assessment to measure maturity beyond what compliance audits showed. The blockchain startup had familiar gaps: weak logging, unencrypted storage, public buckets, trust placed in the client-side application, and no dedicated security team.

Their advice for smaller companies is to cover the basics first: centralized logging, identity federation, budget alerts and one standard deployment path. Larger organizations should plan early, track metrics that show trends over time, and fix problems at the root so the benefits spread across teams.

talks.title: Privacy Impact Assessments - how much privacy is enough?
talks.teaser: Walks through privacy impact assessments, how they differ from security risk assessments, and where they fit in Privacy by Design.
talks.summary:
The talk starts by revisiting how security risk assessments work, using a fictional online merchant that stores card data with weak controls. The speaker walks through estimating likelihood and impact, deciding whether to accept, avoid, transfer or mitigate a risk, and measuring what remains. The core contrast follows: a privacy impact assessment keeps the same loop but puts the harm to individuals at the centre, while the organisation still makes the final decision.

The middle covers several invented scenarios, including a tracking-device platform that sells location-linked data to aggregators and a hiring service whose data may be requested by a foreign government. The fair information practice principles serve as the reference for privacy goals, and the speaker notes that laws name these assessments differently, so context matters. Problematic data actions and privacy harms are catalogued, from economic and reputational damage to psychological and autonomy harms, and controls range from Privacy by Design defaults to pseudonymisation and encryption.

The closing section looks at when to run an assessment, ideally early in development and whenever law requires it, and argues that AppSec practitioners can help with data mapping and privacy threat modeling while legal and risk teams own financial exposure. Legal questions are left to lawyers.

talks.title: Writing Policies That Aren’t Miserable for Everyone Involved
talks.teaser: Explains how splitting one monolithic security policy into audience-specific layers makes policies readable and auditable.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that corporate security and privacy policies are written for lawyers, auditors and HR rather than for the employees who must follow them, so almost nobody reads them. The speaker compares this to aviation pre-flight briefings, where pilots must review a huge volume of material and the regulator has admitted that critical details get lost.

The proposed fix is to split one monolithic policy into layers: a one-page overview with scope, objectives and references, then policy statements and implementation-agnostic standards, then platform-specific guidelines and task-level procedures, each linked up the chain. Employees read only what applies to their job, while a compiled printout still satisfies auditors. Changing one requirement means editing one document, and templates and an FAQ give developers a compliant starting point.

Practical advice includes keeping policy statements short and implementation-agnostic so they survive vendor changes, tying requirements to frameworks or documented risks to make engineering discussions easier, and keeping documentation aligned with the real environment. The overall lesson is to write for the people who apply the policy rather than for auditors alone.
